title.text: Red lights and turns on red

why_how.text: Signals, signs and markings keep traffic orderly, and they bind drivers, riders, bicyclists and pedestrians alike.
A red light means a full stop, and turns on red follow strict conditions that differ for right and left turns.

scenario.text: Nia is stopped at a red light on a one-way street and wants to turn left onto a two-way street.

reasoning.text: A left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after a full stop and yield.

result.text: Nia stays stopped until the light changes, because the street she would turn onto is two-way.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking left on red works anywhere right on red does.

correction.text: Right on red is allowed from any street after a stop, while left on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street.

memory_support.text: Right anywhere after a stop; left only one-way to one-way.

prompt.text: Nia, on a one-way street at a red light, wants to turn left onto a two-way street. May she?

answer.text: No. Left on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street.

rationale.text: The left turn on red needs one-way streets on both sides, plus a full stop and yield, so a two-way destination rules it out.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on red lights and turning on red. Signals, signs and markings keep traffic orderly. Cutting through a parking lot or a field to dodge them is illegal, and a police officer's direction overrules every sign and signal. Traffic signals bind drivers, motorcycle riders, bicyclists, moped riders and pedestrians alike, so nobody on the road is exempt. In this lesson we cover where to stop at a red light, when a right turn on red is allowed and when it is banned, the narrow rule for a left turn on red, what a steady red arrow means in Virginia, and why you should check the local law before turning on red in another state.

lines.text: Stop fully at the stop line.
No line: stop before the intersection or crosswalk.
Stay stopped while red, unless a turn is allowed.

narration.text: At a red light, stop fully at the stop line. Where no stop line exists, stop before the intersection or before the crosswalk. Then stay stopped while the light is red, unless a turn is allowed. That last condition is the doorway to the rest of this lesson, because Virginia allows some turns on red and forbids others. The stopping point does not change for a turn: even when you plan to turn on red, the full stop at the line, or before the intersection or crosswalk, comes first. Remember also that a police officer's direction overrules the signal, so if an officer waves you on, the officer's direction is the one that you follow.

lines.text: Watch for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds.

narration.text: A right turn on red needs a full stop first. After the stop, look both ways and yield the right-of-way to pedestrians and traffic, watching for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds. Only then may you turn. There are two places where no right turn on red is allowed at all: where No Turn on Red signs stand, and where a red arrow points right. So the right-on-red rule has a procedure, which is stop, look both ways and yield, and it has two bans, which are the No Turn on Red sign and the red right arrow. When neither ban applies, and you have stopped and yielded, the right turn on red is allowed from any street.

lines.text: Never where signs or a red left arrow forbid it.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers assume that a left turn on red works just like a right turn on red. It does not. A left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after a full stop and a yield, and never where signs or a red left arrow forbid it. Right on red is allowed from any street after a stop, while left on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street. So before turning left on red, check both streets. If either one carries two-way traffic, the left turn on red is not allowed, and you wait for the signal to change.

lines.text: Steady red arrow: stop and stay stopped.
Turn only where a red-arrow-after-stop sign is posted.
Other states: learn the local law.

narration.text: A steady red arrow means stop and stay stopped in that direction, unless Right on Red Arrow After Stop or Left on Red Arrow After Stop signs are posted. Virginia otherwise bans turns at red arrows. So at a red arrow, the sign makes the difference: without one of those permissive signs, you stay stopped until the arrow changes. Finally, red-light and red-arrow turn rules differ by state, so learn the local law before turning on red outside Virginia. The rules in this lesson are Virginia's rules, and the manual itself warns you not to assume another state has the same ones when you travel there.

lines.text: Turning left onto a two-way street.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Nia is stopped at a red light on a one-way street, and she wants to turn left onto a two-way street. May she turn left on red? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. A left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after a full stop and a yield. Because the street Nia would turn onto carries two-way traffic, the condition is not met, and she stays stopped until the light changes. If both streets were one-way, she could turn after a full stop and a yield, as long as no sign or red left arrow forbids it.

lines.text: Right on red: stop, look, yield.
Left on red: one-way to one-way only.

narration.text: To close the lesson, here are the red light rules together. Stop fully at the stop line, or before the intersection or crosswalk where no line exists, and stay stopped while red unless a turn is allowed. A right turn on red needs a full stop, a look both ways and a yield, and it is banned where No Turn on Red signs stand or a red arrow points right. A left turn on red is allowed only from one-way onto one-way. A steady red arrow means stay stopped unless a red-arrow-after-stop sign is posted. And outside Virginia, learn the local law first. The memory line is: right anywhere after a stop, left only one-way to one-way.

why_how.text: Flashing reds require a stop and a yield before going, while yellow signals warn or slow you without the same stop.
Steady and flashing versions of the same color mean different things, which is a frequent source of mistakes.

scenario.text: Leo reaches a flashing red light with no other traffic in sight.

reasoning.text: At a flashing red light you stop fully, yield to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians, and go only when clear.

result.text: Leo stops fully, checks that the way is clear, and then proceeds.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a flashing red like a flashing yellow and rolling through.

correction.text: Flashing red demands a full stop plus a yield before going, while flashing yellow demands no stop at all.

memory_support.text: Flashing red stops you; flashing yellow slows you.

prompt.text: Leo sees a flashing red light and no traffic. May he slow down and drive through without stopping?

answer.text: No. A flashing red light requires a full stop and a yield before going.

rationale.text: Flashing red demands a full stop plus a yield, and only flashing yellow lets you proceed without stopping.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on flashing and yellow signals. The key idea in this lesson is that a steady signal and a flashing signal of the same color mean different things. We will start with the flashing red light and the flashing red arrow, compare them with the steady red signals from the last lesson, and then work through the steady yellow, the flashing yellow, and the flashing yellow arrow. Along the way we will set up three contrasts that the exam likes to test: steady red against flashing red, steady yellow against flashing yellow, and flashing red against flashing yellow. Keep listening for the word stop, because that is where the differences show up.

lines.text: Flashing red light: stop, yield, go when clear.
Flashing red arrow: stop, yield, then arrow direction.

narration.text: At a flashing red light, stop fully, yield to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians, and go only when the way is clear. At a railroad crossing, always stop, even with no train in sight. A flashing red arrow works the same way for one direction: stop fully, yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, and move in the arrow direction only when clear. Now compare the steady versions. A steady red light holds you stopped for its whole phase, while a flashing red light lets you proceed once stopped, yielded and clear. A steady red arrow holds you stopped with Virginia banning the turn, while a flashing red arrow releases you after a stop and yield when clear.

lines.text: Unsafe to stop or already inside: pass through cautiously.

narration.text: A steady yellow light or arrow warns that the signal is changing. If you have not entered the intersection, stop. If stopping is unsafe, or you are already inside the intersection, pass through cautiously. And never speed up. That last instruction matters: a steady yellow is a warning that the signal is changing, never a signal to hurry. The steady yellow orders a stop from outside the intersection, with a careful pass-through allowed only when stopping is unsafe or you are already inside. Speeding up is never part of the rule, so if you have not entered and can stop safely, the steady yellow means you stop.

title.text: Flashing yellow is not a stop

lines.text: Flashing yellow: slow down, proceed with caution.
Flashing red: full stop and yield.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with caution, and it marks a spot with a higher-than-normal hazard. It does not require a stop. A flashing red does. Flashing red demands a full stop plus a yield before going, while flashing yellow demands no stop at all. And compare the two yellows: a steady yellow orders a stop from outside the intersection, while a flashing yellow orders only slower, cautious travel. If you mix these up, you will either stop where the rule only asked you to slow down, or roll through a flashing red where the rule requires a full stop and a yield.

Here is a quick check: Leo reaches a flashing red light and there is no other traffic in sight. May he slow down and drive through without stopping? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. At a flashing red light you stop fully, yield to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians, and go only when clear. The empty road does not change the rule; Leo still makes the full stop and then proceeds once he sees it is clear. Slowing down without stopping is what a flashing yellow allows, because flashing yellow demands no stop at all. So the color decides it: flashing red stops you, and flashing yellow slows you.

lines.text: Turn in the arrow direction when clear.
Yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.
Check for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds.

narration.text: To close, the flashing yellow arrow. At a flashing yellow arrow, turn in the arrow direction when clear, yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, and checking for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds. Unlike a flashing red arrow, it does not require a full stop first, but it does require you to yield. To recap the lesson: flashing red lights and arrows mean stop, yield and go when clear, and at railroad crossings you always stop. A steady yellow means stop if you have not entered, and never speed up. A flashing yellow means slow down and use caution. The memory line is: flashing red stops you, and flashing yellow slows you.

why_how.text: A green light lets you go only when clear, and a turn without a green arrow means yielding.
Signals with no lights, lane-use signals and the pedestrian hybrid beacon each have their own rule.

scenario.text: Grace drives toward an intersection where the traffic signals are completely dark, and no officer is present.

reasoning.text: When signals show no lights at all, you stop and cross as at an all-way stop, unless an officer or authorized person directs traffic or portable stop signs are in use.

result.text: Grace stops and crosses as she would at an all-way stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a green light gives you the right to turn ahead of oncoming traffic and pedestrians.

correction.text: Turning on a plain green light without an arrow means yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, while a green arrow in your direction means going when clear.

memory_support.text: Red X never, yellow X leave, green arrow drive.

prompt.text: A yellow X appears over the lane you are driving in. What should you do?

answer.text: Leave that lane as soon as it is safe.

rationale.text: A yellow X orders a safe exit from the lane, while a red X bans the lane entirely and a green arrow opens it.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on green signals, dark signals and lane-use signals. Green does not mean you may simply go: you go only when clear, and a turn without a green arrow comes with a duty to yield. Then we will look at what to do when the signals show no lights at all, the three lane signals that hang over individual lanes, which are the red X, the yellow X and the green arrow, and finally the pedestrian hybrid beacon, which runs through its own sequence of yellow and red lights. Each of these has a rule that the manual states plainly, and the lane signals in particular are easy to confuse unless you learn them as a set of three.

lines.text: No green arrow: yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.
Let pedestrians in the street finish crossing.

narration.text: At a green light or a green arrow, go only when the way is clear. Turning without a green arrow means yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, and letting any pedestrian already in the street finish crossing. Compare the two kinds of green when you turn. Turning on a plain green light without an arrow means yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, while a green arrow in your direction means going when clear. So a plain green light lets you turn, but it does not put you first. If a pedestrian is in the street as you begin your turn, the rule is simple: you let that person finish crossing before you complete the turn.

lines.text: No lights: stop and cross as at an all-way stop.
Unless an officer or authorized person directs traffic.
Or portable stop signs are in use.

narration.text: Sometimes signals show no lights at all. When that happens, stop and cross as you would at an all-way stop. There are two exceptions. If an officer or another authorized person is directing traffic, follow that direction. And if portable stop signs are in use, follow them. Otherwise, a dark signal is handled as an all-way stop. Remember the rule for all-way stops from the signs part of this section: every approach stops, and when two drivers arrive together, the driver on the left yields. A dark signal never means the intersection is uncontrolled, so the safe habit is to treat it as a full stop on every approach.

lines.text: Red X: never drive in that lane.
Yellow X or downward arrow: leave when safe.
Green arrow: lane open; turn arrow: enter only to turn.

narration.text: Here is the trap: three lane signals, three different meanings. Never drive in a lane marked with a red X signal. A yellow X, or a yellow diagonal downward arrow, means leave that lane as soon as it is safe. A green arrow opens its lane to driving, while a one-way or two-way turn arrow lets you enter only to turn in the arrow direction. Put together, a red X bans its lane entirely, a yellow X orders a safe exit from the lane, and a green arrow opens the lane. The red and yellow X look alike from far away, so learn the colors: red means never, and yellow means get out of the lane when it is safe.

lines.text: Solid double red: drivers stop, walkers cross.
Alternating flashing reds: go with caution once clear.

narration.text: A pedestrian hybrid beacon runs in a set order. First flashing yellow, then solid yellow, then solid double red with the walk signal, while drivers must stop. Then come alternating flashing reds, which release drivers with caution once the crosswalk clears. The two red phases are the ones to separate. Solid double reds on a pedestrian beacon hold drivers stopped with walkers crossing, while the later alternating flashing reds release drivers with caution once the crosswalk clears. So during the solid double red you wait, and during the alternating flashing reds you may go, but only with caution and only after the crosswalk is clear of people.

lines.text: A yellow X over your lane.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving and a yellow X appears over the lane you are in. What should you do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to leave that lane as soon as it is safe. A yellow X, or a yellow diagonal downward arrow, orders a safe exit from the lane. It is not the red X, which means never drive in that lane at all, and it is not the green arrow, which opens the lane to driving. Notice the words as soon as it is safe: the yellow X does not ask for a sudden swerve, it asks you to move out of the lane safely. Red X never, yellow X leave, green arrow drive.

lines.text: Green: go when clear, yield on turns.
Red X, yellow X, green arrow.

narration.text: To close the lesson: at a green light or arrow, go only when clear, and when turning without a green arrow, yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians and let any pedestrian in the street finish crossing. When signals show no lights at all, stop and cross as at an all-way stop, unless an officer directs traffic or portable stop signs are used. Over the lanes, a red X means never drive there, a yellow X means leave when safe, and a green arrow opens the lane. At a pedestrian hybrid beacon, solid double reds hold you stopped, and alternating flashing reds release you with caution once the crosswalk clears. The memory line: red X never, yellow X leave, green arrow drive.

why_how.text: A sign's color and shape warn early: shape may show in heavy fog, and color reads from far off before the message.
Each color pairing carries a meaning, and the octagon and triangle carry the stop and yield rules.

scenario.text: Sam sees an orange sign with black lettering ahead.

reasoning.text: Orange with black warns in construction zones, while pink with black warns at incidents.

result.text: Sam expects a construction zone ahead.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the triangle means the same full stop as the octagon.

correction.text: The eight-sided octagon always commands a full stop, while the triangle commands only slowing with a stop as needed.

memory_support.text: Eight sides stop; three sides yield.

prompt.text: You see a pink sign with black lettering. What is it warning you about?

rationale.text: Pink with black warns at incidents, while orange with black warns through construction zones.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on sign colors and shapes. A sign's color and shape warn you early. Shape alone may show in heavy fog, and color reads from far off, before the message on the sign does. That is why it pays to know what each color and shape means: you can start reacting before you can read a single word. In this lesson we will match each color pairing to its meaning, from red and white to pink and black, and then look closely at the two shapes with the strongest rules: the eight-sided octagon, which always means stop, and the triangle, which means yield. We finish with the all-way stop rule for drivers who arrive together.

lines.text: Red with white: stop, yield, do not, no.

narration.text: Start with the colors that set rules or warn. Red with white means stop, yield, do not, and no. Black with white carries regulatory law. Yellow with black warns. A strong yellow-green is reserved for school, pedestrian and bicyclist activity. Put more simply, black with white states a law to obey, yellow with black warns of a hazard, and red with white orders stop, yield or no. When you see one of these colors from a distance, you already know the kind of message that is coming: an order, a law, a hazard ahead, or activity by schoolchildren, pedestrians or bicyclists. That early knowledge is the whole point of the color system.

Now the remaining colors. Green with white gives destinations. Blue with white gives motorist services. Brown with white marks historic or cultural interests. Orange with black warns in construction zones, and pink with black warns at incidents. The last two are easy to swap, so here is the contrast stated directly: orange with black warns through construction zones, while pink with black warns at incidents. Both are warnings printed in black, so the background color is what tells you which situation lies ahead. Green, blue and brown, on the other hand, give you information rather than warnings: where you are going, what services exist, and what places of interest are nearby.

lines.text: Triangle: slow down, be ready to stop, let others pass.
Stop only as needed at the triangle.

narration.text: Here is the trap: the octagon and the triangle are not two versions of the same rule. The eight-sided octagon always means stop. Halt fully at the sign, line, crosswalk or curb, and wait for a clear way. The triangle means yield: slow down, stand ready to stop, and let vehicles, pedestrians and bicyclists pass first. So the octagon always commands a full stop, while the triangle commands only slowing, with a stop as needed. At a triangle you stop only as needed to let others pass, but at an octagon only slowing down never satisfies the rule. The memory line: eight sides stop, three sides yield.

Here is a quick check: you see a pink sign with black lettering ahead. What is it warning you about? Work it out before reading on. The answer is an incident. Pink with black warns at incidents, while orange with black warns through construction zones. Both are warnings with black lettering, so the background color is what separates them. If you answered a construction zone, you were thinking of orange. Try the rest of the set too: green with white gives destinations, blue with white gives motorist services, and brown with white marks historic or cultural interests. Being able to name each color quickly is exactly the skill this lesson is building.

lines.text: Every approach stops at all-way or four-way signs.
Ties: the driver on the left yields.
Color first, shape second, message third.

narration.text: To close, the all-way stop. At all-way or four-way stop signs, every approach stops, and when drivers tie, the driver on the left yields. To recap the lesson: color and shape warn early, with shape showing in fog and color reading from far off. Red with white orders stop, yield, do not or no; black with white states regulatory law; yellow with black warns; and yellow-green marks school, pedestrian and bicyclist activity. Green gives destinations, blue gives services, brown marks historic or cultural interests, orange warns in construction zones, and pink warns at incidents. The octagon always means a full stop, and the triangle means yield.
